about: A fast web browser that runs without a screen, made for bots and AI agents that read websites.

prs.title: Typing in a box now tells the page the value changed
prs.broken: Pages often wait for a 'changed' signal before they check, save or filter what was typed. Chrome sends it when you leave the box or press Enter. This browser never sent it, so those pages never saw the typed text.
prs.changed: The browser now remembers the value from before the typing and sends the signal on leaving the box or pressing Enter, if the value is different, as Chrome does.
prs.matters: Forms that check or save what you type now work for bots too.

prs.title: Filter and sort forms now send the new choice
prs.broken: When a form like 'sort by' was sent from a page whose address already held choices, the browser added the new choice instead of replacing the old one. With a '#' in the address, the form was never sent.
prs.changed: The browser now swaps the old choices for the form's and keeps the '#' part at the end, as the web standard says and Chrome does.
prs.matters: Bots that filter, sort or search through forms land on the page they asked for.

prs.title: A '?' after the '#' in a link no longer changes the address
prs.broken: Many web apps put a '?' after the '#' in their links. The browser read it as part of the real address, so edited links went somewhere else and servers were told text meant to stay in the browser.
prs.changed: The browser now only looks for the '?' before the '#', like Chrome does.
prs.matters: Links in these apps go where they should, and the private part of the address stays private.

prs.title: Searches for forms and links now ignore letter case, like Chrome
prs.broken: Pages often write things like method="POST". Searching the page for forms with method=post found nothing, though Chrome finds them, so bots missed forms and links.
prs.changed: For the attributes where the web standard says case doesn't matter, the search now ignores it.
prs.matters: Bots and test tools find the same parts of a page that Chrome does.

prs.title: Saved logins now survive being restored
prs.broken: Programs that save a logged-in session and load it later got back a logged-out one. The browser misread the login cookies' 'no end date' mark as 'expired' and dropped them.
prs.changed: The browser now keeps those cookies until the session ends, as Chrome does.
prs.matters: Bots can log in once and reuse that login, instead of ending up signed out.

prs.title: Dropdown choices now send clean text
prs.broken: Dropdown choices kept the extra spaces and line breaks from the page's source code. Forms sent the server garbled values, and picking a choice by name found nothing.
prs.changed: The browser now trims and squeezes that extra space, as the web standard says.
prs.matters: Servers get the same form answers they would get from Chrome.

prs.title: Ctrl+A now selects all the text in a box
prs.broken: Pressing Ctrl+A in a text box did nothing. Programs that clear a field by selecting all and typing over it ended up with the old text plus the new.
prs.changed: The browser now selects everything in the box on Ctrl+A, like Chrome on Linux.
prs.matters: A common way scripts clear and refill form fields now works.

prs.title: A missing table feature no longer breaks page searches
prs.broken: Pages couldn't ask a table for its rows. Playwright, a popular tool for driving browsers, needs that, so on some pages with tables every search for a heading or button crashed.
prs.changed: I added the list of rows, in the order the web standard sets out.
prs.matters: Playwright scripts that find links, buttons and headings by what they are now work on those pages.

prs.title: Error messages from a page now reach the program
prs.broken: When code run on a page failed, the program controlling the browser got an empty error message, or just 'undefined', instead of the real one Chrome gives.
prs.changed: The browser now labels page objects correctly, so real errors keep their message.
prs.matters: Developers see what actually went wrong instead of a blank error.

prs.title: Deleting a cookie now actually deletes it
prs.broken: Sites often delete a cookie (a small note a site stores in the browser) by giving it a 1970 expiry date ending in 'UTC'. The browser misread that, so the cookie stayed.
prs.changed: I taught the browser to read dates ending in 'UTC', so those cookies are removed as in Chrome.
prs.matters: Log-out and cookie-consent code that clears cookies this way now works.

prs.title: The browser's own tests stop hiding failures
prs.broken: In the project's test suite, a test that crashed after its first check passed still counted as passed. One test had been quietly skipping its later checks this way.
prs.changed: I made a crash anywhere in a test count as a failure, and fixed the test it had been hiding.
prs.matters: Behind-the-scenes work: future bugs can't slip past tests that only look like they passed.

prs.title: Searches inside news feeds and drawings now find items
prs.broken: Programs looking up parts of a page by name came up empty in two cases: inside RSS news feeds, and for some drawing elements with capital letters in their names.
prs.changed: I made the browser match those names properly; one small upper/lowercase difference from Chrome is left.
prs.matters: Scripts that read news feeds or graphics on a page now find what is there.

prs.title: Custom page elements are now told apart by name
prs.broken: Sites can invent their own element types, like a 'card'. Asked for 'the second card', the browser lumped all invented types together and picked the wrong one, or none.
prs.changed: The browser now treats each invented element name as its own type, as Chrome does.
prs.matters: Scripts that pick the first, second or last of a kind of item now get the right one.

prs.title: The page clock now reports the real date
prs.broken: A page asking when it was opened got the time since the computer started, not the real date and time, so its date math was off by decades.
prs.changed: The browser now records the real clock time when a page opens and reports that.
prs.matters: Page scripts that log or measure time get correct timestamps.

prs.title: A space before a closing bracket is no longer an error
prs.broken: Page lookups like 'every odd item in a list' failed with an error if there was a space before the closing bracket, even though the rules allow it.
prs.changed: The browser now skips spaces there, as the styling rules allow.
prs.matters: Small fix: valid page code written with extra spaces no longer stops with an error.

prs.title: Clearing text no longer writes the word 'null'
prs.broken: When a page cleared an element's text by setting it to 'nothing' (null), the browser showed the word 'null' instead of empty text.
prs.changed: The browser now treats 'nothing' as empty text, as the web standard says.
prs.matters: Small fix, but pages no longer show a stray 'null' where text should be blank.

prs.title: Timers with a negative delay now go off
prs.broken: A page timer set with a negative or very large delay was misread as about 49 days, so it never went off. Chrome runs it right away.
prs.changed: The browser now treats such delays as zero, as the web standard says.
prs.matters: Page code that schedules work this way now runs instead of silently waiting.

prs.title: The browser now knows which fields can be typed in
prs.broken: Asked which form fields can be typed into, the browser also counted checkboxes and disabled boxes, and said no field was read-only.
prs.changed: I made it follow the web standard's rules for what counts as editable.
prs.matters: Scripts and page styles that treat locked fields differently now see the same fields Chrome does.

prs.title: Saving a page's code no longer drops template parts
prs.broken: Pages can hold hidden 'template' blocks used to build content later. When the browser turned a page back into code, those blocks came out empty.
prs.changed: The browser now writes out what is inside templates, as the web standard says.
prs.matters: Saved copies of pages, including the browser's own page-dump command, keep all their content.

prs.title: Backspace, Tab and the arrow keys work now
prs.broken: When a program typed on a page, keys that don't type a letter (Backspace, Delete, arrows, Escape) were silently ignored. Pressing Backspace in a text box deleted nothing.
prs.changed: The browser now handles those key presses the same way Chrome does.
prs.matters: Scripts that fill in forms behave the same here as in a normal browser.

prs.title: Form fields are checked as valid or invalid the way browsers do
prs.broken: Web pages can style or find form fields that are filled in wrong. Lightpanda only noticed empty required fields, so a bad email address or a number below the limit counted as valid.
prs.changed: I made it use every rule a field has, like format, pattern, limits and custom messages, and leave out disabled fields.
prs.matters: Scripts and tests that look for invalid fields get the same answer as in Chrome.

prs.title: Sliders and color pickers start with their default value
prs.broken: A slider or color picker on a web form with no starting value was empty instead of its default, the middle of the range or black. Forms sent an empty field.
prs.changed: I made these fields start at their default, and go back to it when a form is reset.
prs.matters: Forms filled in by Lightpanda send the same values a regular browser would.
